newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks in dilemma over support for Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks in dilemma over support for Thailand.

text.p: Japanese banks, already heavily exposed to Thailand, are torn between a desire to play a key role in financial support for the country and worries about how their money will be spent, bankers say.
Still striving to clean up massive bad loans at home, the banks do not want their money to be used for the ailing financial sector in Thailand.
But at the same time they feel a strong commitment is necessary to maintain their presence in the region, they said.

"There are mixed feelings among banks," said one banking source. "Some banks are even trying to take advantage of the crisis to score points with the Thai authorities for future business opportunities."
Thailand said earlier this week that it was seeking $12 billion to $15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stabilise its economy.
The IMF will convene a meeting of interested countries and multilateral institutions in Tokyo on August 11 to discuss a financing package for Thailand.
The focus is now shifting to how much Japanese commercial banks and other foreign banks will provide to the rescue package.
Officials of Japanese banks said they have not received any formal requests for assistance.

But a senior official at one major Japanese bank said the framework of private banks' financing could be set later this month after Monday's meeting and an IMF board meeting in mid-August. There is talk that private banks from Japan and other nations will shoulder a total burden of $5.0 billion.

A Japanese government source said it was highly likely Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya would meet officials of private Japanese banks before he leaves Tokyo on Tuesday after attending the IMF talks.
Banking sources said two big Japanese banks -- Sakura Bank and Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi -- are expected to play a leading role, but help could be needed from foreign banks.
"In order to live up to terms of loans that the Thai government will seek, it will be necessary to have U.S. money-centre banks participate in lending," said the bank official.

Credit ratings of Japanese banks have been downgraded due to their bad loan problems after the collapse of Japan's "bubble" economy in the early 1990s and they are forced to pay higher costs in raising funds overseas than Western banks.
Banking sources said Thailand would be delighted to receive as much as money it could get to deal with a severe economic crisis after a decade of high growth.
Its financial sector has been hard hit by a liquidity crunch and rising non-performing loans due to over-exposure to non-productive industry, especially the property sector, analysts say.

"The IMF believes $12 billion to 15 billion would be enough to help stabilise the Thai economy, but there are doubts if public money alone can satisfy the financial markets," the bank official said, adding that private money was also needed.
"But the big question is whether private money will be used for the bad loan problems or as compensation for a shortfall in tax revenues," he added.
The IMF's money is expected to be mainly used for correcting the Thai current account deficit.
Thailand has nearly $90 billion in foreign currency debt, with Japanese banks accounting for nearly half of it.
Major Japanese commercial banks, faced with moribund demand for funds at home, have looked to Asian nations as the best place to lend money since the early 1990s.
Japanese bankers said that since the bulk of the money had been lent to subsidiaries of Japanese firms operating in Thailand, they did not have a major problem.
But analysts said prolonged economic turmoil and depreciation of the Thai currency may hurt profits of Japanese subsidiaries and bring yet more bad loans to Japanese banks.
Many finance firms were recently ordered by the Thai authorities to suspend their operations, including some in which capital is held by Japanese banks.
